Deleting Your Google History vs Removing Yourself from Google: What Each One Does

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Clearing your Google or Chrome history deletes the record of what you searched and visited; it does not remove a single page about you from Google's search results. The first is a privacy setting in your own account, the second requires the website owner or Google to act on content published by others. Confusing the two is one of the most common misunderstandings we see among Italian clients.

Two different problems: your activity and information about you

Your search history is data about what you do, stored in your Google account and your browser. Information about you is content that other people publish on websites, which Google indexes and shows to anyone who searches for your name. Different tools and rules apply to each.

Your history and account dataInformation about you online
Where it livesYour Google account and your devicesThird-party websites indexed by Google
Who can see itYou, and anyone with access to your account or deviceAnyone who searches
Who can delete itYou, in a few clicksThe website owner, or Google through delisting
Legal basis neededNoneGoogle policies, GDPR, court decisions

Both matter for privacy, but only the second one shapes your reputation. The sections below explain how to handle each correctly.

How to clear Google search history

To clear Google search history, open My Activity (myactivity.google.com) while signed in, choose Delete and select a time range or all time. Searches made in the Google app, on google.it and through Google Assistant are stored there when Web & App Activity is turned on.

A clean history is easier to keep if you set it up once:

  1. Go to your Google account, then Data and privacy, then Web & App Activity.
  2. Decide whether to keep the setting on, pause it, or turn on auto-delete for activity older than 3, 18 or 36 months.
  3. Review the sub-option that includes Chrome history and activity from sites and apps that use Google services.
  4. In My Activity, delete individual items, a date range or everything stored so far.
  5. In the Google app on your phone, use the option to delete the last 15 minutes of searches when you need a quick clean-up.

Pausing the setting stops new searches from being saved to your account, although Google may still process some data temporarily for security and to deliver the service. Searches made while signed out are not tied to your account history, but they can still be linked to your browser through cookies.

How to delete Chrome history

To delete Chrome history on a computer, press Ctrl+Shift+Delete (Cmd+Shift+Delete on a Mac), choose the time range and select browsing history, cookies and cached files as needed. On Android and iPhone the same option is under History in the Chrome menu.

Two details are often overlooked. If Chrome sync is active, deleting history on one device removes it from all devices signed in to the same account, which is useful but surprising to some users. Deleting cookies also signs you out of most websites and resets their preferences. For shared or work computers in an Italian office, using a separate Chrome profile or a guest window avoids the problem entirely.

How to delete your data from Google

Beyond search history, your account holds emails, photos, location history, YouTube activity and more. You can delete your data from Google service by service in the account settings, download a copy first with Google Takeout, or delete the whole account if you no longer need it.

For users in Italy and the rest of the EU, Google Ireland acts as data controller and is bound by the GDPR. You have the right to access your data (art. 15), to have it erased (art. 17) and to object to certain processing (art. 21). Most requests are handled through the account tools, but formal requests can also be made through Google's privacy contact forms, and if they are not handled correctly you can complain to the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, which coordinates with the Irish authority under the GDPR's cross-border rules.

Deleting your history protects what you do online. It does nothing to change what the internet says about you.

Why clearing history does not change what others see

Search results for your name are built from the public web, not from your account. When a client in Milan or a recruiter in Rome types your name, Google shows them pages published by news sites, directories, social networks and review platforms, regardless of anything stored in your own history.

Your own results may even look slightly different from theirs, because Google personalises some results based on your location, language and past activity. That is why people sometimes clear their history, search for their name and conclude that a negative article has disappeared, while others still see it at the top. To check what the public sees, search in a private window, signed out, and on a different device or network if possible. Things that remain visible after any history clean-up include:

  • news articles and blog posts that mention you;
  • reviews, forum threads and comments about you or your business;
  • public profiles on social networks, directories and professional registers;
  • images published on other websites and indexed in Google Images;
  • autocomplete suggestions generated from what other people search.

What to do when the problem is information about you

If the goal is to change what appears when someone searches your name, the work moves from your account settings to the content itself. The usual sequence is to ask the website owner to remove or update the page, then use Google's own tools and, where the law allows, a delisting request.

Google's “Results about you” tool handles pages that show contact details such as your phone number or home address. Outdated or irrelevant personal information can be the subject of a right-to-be-forgotten request (diritto all'oblio) under GDPR art. 17 and the Google Spain ruling (C-131/12), and content already deleted by the site owner can be cleared from the results with the outdated content tool in Search Console.
